content: In 2018, a core outcome set for maternal infectious morbidity related to cesarean delivery was proposed. This was based on a systematic review of 452 trials and a Delphi survey involving 40 review authors. The proposed outcomes included endometritis (as the primary outcome), maternal mortality, wound infection, wound complications, febrile morbidity, and neonatal morbidity. A systematic review of 46 trials comparing different antibiotic classes for infection prevention during cesarean sections found that only two studies reported cost outcomes. One study, conducted in two tertiary hospitals in Nigeria, compared the effectiveness of ceftriaxone (a cephalosporin) with a triple-drug regimen (metronidazole, ampicillin, cloxacillin, and gentamicin). The study reported no difference in hospital stay duration or maternal outcomes but found that ceftriaxone was less expensive ($9 versus $15 for the triple regimen). The authors concluded that the cheaper single-dose antibiotic was as effective as the more expensive triple regimen. However, the study was assessed as low quality using the Consensus Health Economic Criteria (CHEC) checklist. Another study from the USA, included in the Cochrane review, did not provide specific cost data due to incomplete reporting. However, it estimated the cost of failure for prophylactic antibiotics to prevent post-cesarean infections at $5,026 (in 1986), based on hospital charges, laboratory tests, drug costs, and other associated expenses. This value was applied to the failure rates of different antibiotics, with costs ranging from $140,833 for ampicillin to $26,358 for piperacillin per 100 patients. The study was also rated as low quality. A 2017 systematic review assessed cost analyses for prophylactic antibiotics in preventing surgical site infections, including cesarean sections, but found no additional direct evidence comparing different antibiotic classes. An updated literature search in May 2019 did not yield further evidence. The administration of intravenous antibiotics for cesarean sections requires skilled healthcare professionals trained in safe injection practices, hand hygiene, and the management of side effects. Refresher training on antimicrobial stewardship and resistance is also recommended. Necessary resources include sterile equipment, hand hygiene supplies, and proper disposal systems for sharps. The availability of antibiotics significantly impacts equitable access, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. A study of 13,561 healthcare facilities in such settings found that fewer than 50% stocked 17 priority antibiotics. For example, third-generation cephalosporins like ceftriaxone and cefotaxime were available in only 50% and 8% of facilities, respectively. However, availability may be higher in higher-level facilities where cesarean sections are performed. A systematic review on the perspectives of women and providers regarding antibiotic prophylaxis at birth identified several factors influencing provider practices. These included concerns about infection risk, unnecessary antibiotic use, side effects, medicalization of birth, and antimicrobial resistance. Some providers were motivated by fear of postpartum infections and medico-legal risks, while others considered cost-effectiveness and affordability when prescribing antibiotics. There was no evidence on women’s perspectives regarding the acceptability or feasibility of this intervention. In summary, various antibiotic classes have been evaluated for preventing infections during cesarean sections, but there is insufficient evidence to determine which class is superior. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that minimally anti-staphylococcal cephalosporins (third generation) may increase endometritis rates compared to non-anti-staphylococcal penicillins. Evidence on neonatal outcomes, maternal side effects, well-being, satisfaction, and antimicrobial resistance is lacking. Cost-effectiveness likely varies, and while antibiotic regimens are generally acceptable and feasible, their impact on equity remains uncertain.
